Chapter 4: Dispelling Myths About Healing and Progress
So, now that we've built a foundation of honesty and responsibility, it’s time to talk about something that trips up a lot of us—the myths we hear about healing and self-improvement.
Ever notice how people often say recovery from trauma or loss should follow a neat, predictable path? That if you just give it enough time, or keep a positive attitude, you'll naturally bounce back and be happy again? Well, let’s be real—healing is rarely that tidy.
In truth, the process is usually messy, unpredictable, and full of ups and downs. Progress shows up in starts and stops—sometimes you’re moving forward, and other times, it feels like you’re standing still or even sliding back. There’s no universal timeline, and it almost never looks like the simple stages you might see in self-help books.
One of the biggest myths out there is that “time heals all wounds.” Sure, time can soften the sharpest pain, but it doesn’t guarantee real healing. Some hurts stay with us for years, and some losses never quite go away. If you expect time alone to fix everything, you might end up frustrated—or worse, blaming yourself if things don’t get better as quickly as you hoped.
Here’s another common idea: that positive thinking is all you need to get through tough times. Now, don’t get me wrong—optimism can help. But forcing yourself to always “look on the bright side” can backfire. Sometimes, it just makes it harder to process what you’re really feeling or to grieve in a way that’s actually healthy.
So, what does genuine healing look like? Well, it often means letting yourself feel pain and discomfort, instead of pushing it down or pretending it isn’t there. It’s about accepting that hard days and setbacks are a normal part of the journey. And when things get heavy, it’s okay—actually, it’s wise—to reach out for support without feeling ashamed.
Think about someone dealing with the end of a long-term relationship. Friends might say things like, “Just move on,” or “Find someone new.” They mean well, but advice like that can feel like pressure to get over it fast. In reality, heartbreak is personal. There’s no standard timeline. The right way is whatever works for you.
Another myth? That healing means going back to exactly who you were before. But some experiences really do change us, sometimes in ways we never expected. The goal isn’t to erase the past—it’s to find a way to live with it, and maybe even grow from it.
You might picture this like carrying a heavy stone. At first, it feels impossible to move forward with that weight. Over time, the stone doesn’t get any lighter. What changes is you—you get stronger and better at carrying it. The burden is still there, but it doesn’t have to shape every moment of your life.
Letting go of these myths is a huge act of self-compassion. When you stop expecting things to be simple or quick, it’s easier to accept the highs and lows of healing, without judging yourself. That’s when real progress happens—even if it’s slow, or a little uneven.
And remember, traditional advice, even when it’s well-meaning, isn’t always what you need. Everyone’s path looks different. What matters most is finding what feels meaningful and helpful for you, not just following someone else’s idea of recovery.
By questioning these myths, you give yourself permission to approach healing with patience and a sense of realism. It’s not about giving up hope—it’s about embracing the complicated, winding process of recovery, and trusting in your own resilience to see you through.
